newsitem.title: CHINA: Large crowds turn out to greet PLA in HK.
newsitem.headline: Large crowds turn out to greet PLA in HK.

text.p: Large crowds braved driving rain on Tuesday to welcome Chinese troops streaming into Hong Kong after the end of more than 150 years of British rule.
"We welcome the troops very much because this is the stamp of sovereignty," said an elderly man near this frontier crossing point.
More than 4,000 troops from the People's Liberation Army (PLA) poured into Hong Kong in long convoys of open trucks and in armoured personnel carriers (APCs) with machineguns mounted on turrets.
"We are more curious and excited than we are welcoming. We are here mainly because we have been partying all night," said one young man in the crowd.
All-night parties have swept this territory of 6.4 million people to celebrate the handing over of Hong Kong to communist China at midnight on Monday.
Garlands were hung around the necks of PLA officers. People stepped forward to embrace soldiers, whose deployment has been sharply criticised by pro-democracy activists in Hong Kong.
Dancing girls in bright costumes lined the streets and local villagers stretched along the roads for hundreds of metres.
Asked if they were afraid of the stone-faced PLA troops, one woman dancer said: "The PLA aren't supposed to turn their heads towards us, are they?"
Some of the soldiers waved but in a disciplined manner.
They were followed by 21 APCs and a half dozen communications trucks with elaborate antennae on the roof. The APCs drew cheers from the crowd.

Pro-democracy activists in Hong Kong have sharply criticised the decision by Beijing to deploy the APCs, saying they brought back memories of the PLA's crushing of student-led protests centred on Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.
A crowd of at least 500 people waited outside the Gun Club Hill Barracks, near a busy Hong Kong shopping district, holding little red Chinese and Hong Kong flags in the rain.
"Of course we are happy. We have been waiting for this day," a 65-year-old woman said. "The British never took care of us and left us to perish during the war."
Chinese warships crossed into Hong Kong waters but only one helicopter was able to fly into the territory. Ten others were grounded by the weather.
Many of the soldiers were armed with assault rifles, but some members of the convoy carried bouquets of red and pink flowers.

Before crossing into Hong Kong the troops stood at attention in the back of uncovered military trucks as throngs of people in ceremonial costumes lined roads to give the Hong Kong garrison a big send-off.
China's top army official told the troops in the border city of Shenzhen to love the people of Hong Kong and protect their prosperity.
"You must respect Hong Kong's social system and the way of living," General Liu Huaqing, vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, told a departure ceremony for the garrison.
The red flag of China flew over the former British military garrison in Hong Kong on Tuesday morning after the PLA planted China's stamp of sovereignty on the territory.
Chinese soldiers stood guard at the gates of the Prince of Wales Barracks, the former British military headquarters on the central Hong Kong waterfront.
The Chinese flag was flying from the garrison within seconds of the British colony being returned to China at a handover ceremony presided over by President Jiang Zemin and Britain's Prince Charles.
Jiang signed a decree on Monday ordering the PLA garrison to begin the defence of Hong Kong at midnight.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright criticised Beijing's decision to send the troops across the border within hours of the resumption of Chinese rule.
"I don't think this is the best way to start off," she said.
